S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.

subtypes.Skin Defects: Excessive preoccupation with practically invisible acne, scars, or complexion.
subtypes.Facial Features: Preoccupation with the shape or size of the nose, eyes, or mouth, which appear normal to others.
subtypes.Asymmetry: Excessive obsession with the face or body not being perfectly symmetrical.
subtypes.Muscle Dysmorphia: The belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular despite being normal or muscular.
subtypes.Specific Body Parts: Obsession that specific parts like hair, teeth, or chest are ugly or abnormal.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.

subtypes.Mirror Checking or Avoidance: Compulsively checking oneself in the mirror frequently or, conversely, avoiding mirrors strictly.
subtypes.Excessive Camouflaging: Spending excessive time and effort to hide perceived flaws using makeup, clothes, hats, or sunglasses.
subtypes.Skin Picking: Picking or manipulating the skin excessively to remove or 'fix' flaws.
subtypes.Reassurance Seeking: Repetitively asking others for confirmation that one's appearance is okay or not strange.
subtypes.Comparing: Constantly comparing one's body parts with those of passersby or celebrities.
subtypes.Seeking Cosmetic Procedures: Repeatedly seeking or receiving plastic surgery or dermatological procedures.

symptom.disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent, excessive preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in physical appearance that are minimal or not observable to others, leading to significant distress or impairment. Individuals commonly engage in repetitive behaviors (such as mirror checking, grooming, camouflaging, seeking reassurance) or mental rituals in response to their appearance concerns. The condition often begins in adolescence or early adulthood, tends to be chronic without treatment, and is associated with substantial social, occupational, and functional impairment, including avoidance of activities and relationships. It is distinguished from normal appearance concerns and from eating disorders by the intensity of preoccupation, the presence of time-consuming rituals, and the focus on specific perceived flaws rather than weight or shape alone.

patient.stressor: Ralph had always been somewhat self‑conscious about his appearance, but after his divorce three years ago and re‑entering the dating scene, his worries about how his face and body looked intensified dramatically. Working as a host in a trendy restaurant where younger, image‑focused staff and social‑media‑savvy guests constantly comment on looks heightened his sense that he appeared "unattractive" and "off" in photos he saw tagged online. Over time he began spending longer and longer getting ready for work and canceling plans with friends or potential dates if he felt he couldn’t get his appearance to look acceptable, which contributed to growing isolation and arguments with his ex‑wife about his unreliability with shared parenting events. After his teenage daughter told him she didn’t want to invite him to her school ceremony because she was worried he’d "freak out" about how he looked and refuse to come again, he became alarmed at how much this preoccupation was affecting his relationship with her and agreed to a psychiatric evaluation recommended by his primary care doctor.
patient.chief_complaint: “I spend so much time trying to fix how I look before I go out that I end up missing things with my family and at work.”

S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.
S067.manifestation: Most days I catch myself staring at my face in the bathroom mirror, convinced my nose is crooked and my skin looks saggy and blotchy, and even though people tell me I look fine for my age, all I can see is this older, lopsided guy who doesn’t belong standing at the front of a hip restaurant full of good‑looking twenty‑somethings taking selfies with me in the background.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.
S068.manifestation: Before every shift or any time I’m supposed to see my kids, I’ll spend an hour or more changing shirts, adjusting the lighting, zooming in on photos of myself, and asking my daughter or coworkers if my face looks weird or if my jaw is drooping, and I’ll keep fussing with it until I’m so worked up and late that I sometimes just cancel or show up halfway through.
